en.title: Numbers and age
en.goal: Count from zero to one hundred and say or ask someone's age.

phrases.scenario: You want to know a new friend's age. What do you ask?
Someone asks your age and you're twenty. What do you answer?
You're introducing your ten-year-old nephew. What do you say about his age?
The waiter asks how many people are in your group, which has ten people. What do you say?

phrases.t: I have two brothers and three sisters.

avoir-age.title: "J'ai vingt ans" — why "ai" and not "suis"?
avoir-age.body: In English we say "I am twenty" or "I'm twenty years old", but in French age always uses the verb avoir (to have): j'ai vingt ans, never "je suis vingt ans". It's a common mistake for people who translate directly from English — it's worth memorizing this structure.

vingt-to-quatrevingts.title: "Vingt" is the base of an odd system
vingt-to-quatrevingts.body: In France, after 69 the numbers jump to a base of 20: 70 is soixante-dix ("sixty-ten"), 80 is quatre-vingts ("four-twenties") — the "vingt" you just learned, multiplied! But it isn't like this everywhere French is spoken.

quel-age-wh-in-situ.title: "Quel âge as-tu ?" also becomes "T'as quel âge ?"
quel-age-wh-in-situ.body: In everyday speech, "tu as" often shrinks to t'as, and the question word ("quel âge") can go at the end of the sentence — t'as quel âge ? instead of "quel âge as-tu ?". In the exercises here, keep using the form "quel âge as-tu ?" — it's the form the exercises ask for.
